title: Automation and New Tasks: How Technology Displaces and Reinstates Labor
pub: Journal of Economic Perspectives, vol. 33, no. 2, pp. 3–30 (Spring 2019); NBER Working Paper 25684 (March 2019)
author: Daron Acemoglu · Pascual Restrepo

dom.t: Work redesign: Jagged capability demands selective deployment

st.t: Task change: Small job effects can widen inequality
st.an: The source provides a useful measure of gross task reallocation and relates task-content changes to industry output, productivity and skill intensity. However, the supplied fragment does not establish the direction, causality or magnitude of employment and inequality effects, so it cannot confirm the cluster’s principal proposition that small net job effects can coexist with widening inequality.
qs: The gross change in task content is defined as the sum of the absolute values of the displacement and reinstatement effects computed in equation (A 13).

Columns        5-6 present results for the change in skill requirements, measured by the share of college educated workers in each industry (from the 1990 US Census and the        pooled 2012-2016 ACS).

st.t: Aggregate productivity: Task speedups shrink during scaling
st.an: The source materially extends the cluster’s task-based account by providing a method for separating substitution effects from changes in task content and, under additional assumptions, decomposing those changes into displacement and reinstatement. This strengthens analysis of how automation and new tasks affect labour outcomes, though it does not address AI-specific adoption, verification or projected productivity gains.
qs: We estimate industry-level change in task content as the residual change in labor share (observed directly in the data) which cannot be explained by the substitution effect.
Under additional assumptions, we can also separate the change in task content into its two components: the displacement and reinstatement effects.

st.t: Employment effects: Task substitution permits stable jobs
st.an: The source accepts the cluster’s central claim that automation does not mechanically determine employment outcomes and materially develops it through a task-based model separating displacement, productivity, reinstatement through new tasks, and sectoral reallocation. It also sharpens the cluster’s qualification that its empirical results concern labor demand through the wage bill, not a distinct employment forecast.
qs: The impact on labor demand can be represented as         Effect of automation on labor demand = Productivity effect + Displacement effect.

Changes is the wage bill will translate into some combination of changes in employment and wages, and the exact division will be affected by the elasticity of labor supply and labor market imperfections, neither of which we model explicitly in this paper (for discussion, see Acemoglu and Restrepo, 2018a, 2018b).

st.t: Job exposure: Which tasks vanish changes outcomes
st.an: The source accepts the distinction between task automation and occupational disappearance and materially develops it through a task-based framework separating displacement, productivity and reinstatement effects. Its postwar decomposition also supports the cluster’s caution that historical resilience does not guarantee future labor demand when automation accelerates and new labor-intensive tasks weaken.
qs: The net impact of automation on labor demand thus depends on how the displacement and productivity effects weigh against each other.

Our empirical decomposition suggests that the slower growth of employment over the last three decades is accounted for by an acceleration in the displacement effect, especially in manufacturing, a weaker reinstatement effect, and slower growth of productivity than in previous decades.

st.t: Legal workflows: Immediate gains create competence risks
st.an: The source reinforces the cluster’s task-reconfiguration framing by supplying a general economic model in which technology changes both task productivity and the allocation of tasks between labour and capital. It materially extends the labour-market analysis through a displacement mechanism, while neither establishing wholesale lawyer replacement nor addressing the cluster’s legal-specific verification, training and competence risks.
qs: New technologies not only increase the productivity of capital and labor at tasks they currently perform, but also impact the allocation of tasks to these factors of production—what we call the task content of production.
Automation changes the task content of production adversely for labor because of a displacement effect—as capital takes over tasks previously performed by labor.

st.t: Work redesign: Jagged capability demands selective deployment
st.an: The source reinforces the cluster’s task-reallocation framing and materially extends it with a framework separating automation’s productivity and displacement effects from the labor-reinstating effect of newly created tasks. Its economy-wide evidence also sharpens the cluster’s labour-risk caveat: redesign need not preserve labour demand unless new human tasks emerge, though it does not address legal-specific capability, verification or workflow evidence.
qs: The impact on labor demand can be represented as         Effect of automation on labor demand = Productivity effect + Displacement effect.
Instead, the displacement effect of automation has been counterbalanced by technologies that create new tasks in which labor has a comparative advantage.

kp.k: Task allocation distinguishes displacement from productivity improvement
kp.d: Acemoglu and Restrepo develop an economy-wide task-based framework, rather than a legal-profession study. Automation transfers tasks previously performed by labor to capital; new labor-intensive tasks expand activities in which humans have a comparative advantage. These changes differ from factor-augmenting technologies that improve performance within existing task allocations.
qs: Tasks are thus the fundamental unit of production, and the factors of production contribute to output by performing these tasks.
Automation enables some of the tasks previously performed by labor to be produced by capital.

kp.k: Automation can reduce labor demand despite raising productivity
kp.d: In the authors’ model, automation reduces an industry's labor share through displacement while increasing productivity and demand for labor in non-automated tasks. Its net labor-demand effect depends on the balance between these forces; productivity growth alone therefore does not establish that employment or wages will rise.
qs: Automation therefore increases the size of the pie, but labor gets a smaller slice.
There is no guarantee that the productivity effect is greater than the displacement effect; some automation technologies can reduce labor demand even as they raise productivity.

kp.d: Under the framework’s adoption and comparative-advantage assumptions, new labor-intensive tasks generate both productivity and reinstatement effects, increasing labor demand and labor share. Historical examples include engineering, management, clerical work, programming, equipment maintenance and computer security. Citing their earlier analysis using Lin’s data, the authors report that about half of employment growth over 1980–2015 occurred in occupations with changed job titles or tasks; this is not an estimate that half of employment growth was caused by AI.
qs: The resulting productivity improvement, together with the change in task content, ensures that labor demand always increases following the introduction of new tasks.
Using data from Lin (2011), Acemoglu and Restrepo (2018a) show that about half of employment growth over 1980-2015 took place in occupations where job titles or tasks performed by workers changed.

kp.k: Marginal automation can be especially unfavorable to labor
kp.d: The authors argue that automation with modest cost savings can displace workers without sufficient productivity gains to offset the loss. They offer automated customer service as an illustrative 'so-so' technology and suggest that some challenging AI applications may fit this category. Effects depend on context: high wages and scarce labor increase potential savings, whereas abundant inexpensive labor limits them. These examples and cross-country explanations are arguments, not measured AI performance results.
qs: Examples of so-so technologies include automated customer service, which has displaced human service representatives but is generally deemed to be low-quality and thus unlikely to have generated large productivity gains.
When wages are high and labor is scarce, automation will generate a strong productivity effect and will tend to raise labor demand.
When wages are low and labor is abundant, automation will bring modest productivity benefits and could end up reducing labor demand.

kp.k: Sectoral reallocation can strengthen or weaken aggregate demand
kp.d: The multi-sector framework adds a composition effect: movement toward sectors with higher labor shares supports aggregate labor demand, while the opposite movement reduces it. The authors interpret nineteenth-century agricultural mechanization as accompanied by favorable reallocation and new industrial tasks. For 1987–2017, however, movement from manufacturing toward services provided little offset because labor shares in contracting and expanding sectors were similar. The appendix qualifies historical comparisons by noting that including proprietors’ income reduces the measured labor-intensity gap.
qs: This reallocation contributes positively to aggregate labor demand when sector j has higher labor share than the contracting sector i, and negatively when the opposite holds.
These findings highlight that unlike the 19th-century mechanization of agriculture, there are no powerful composition effects contributing to labor demand.

kp.k: Wage-bill decomposition infers rather than directly observes tasks
kp.d: Labor demand is operationalized through the wage bill, combining compensation and employment rather than separately estimating job losses and wage changes. The empirical decomposition uses productivity, composition, substitution and task-content components. Task-content changes are residual industry labor-share changes after estimated substitution effects, with baseline elasticity σ = 0.8. The study uses 43 consolidated private-sector industries for 1947–1987 and 61 for 1987–2017, normalizes the wage bill by population, and excludes self-employment income in its baseline.
qs: We focus on the behavior of the wage bill, W L, which captures the total amount employers pay for labor.
We estimate industry-level change in task content as the residual change in labor share (observed directly in the data) which cannot be explained by the substitution effect.
We consolidate the data into 43 industries that covered the private sector and can be tracked consistently over time and across sources.

kp.k: Postwar displacement and reinstatement approximately balanced
kp.d: For 1947–1987, the decomposition reports annual wage-bill-per-capita growth of 2.5%, largely explained by a productivity effect of 2.4% per year. Estimated displacement reduced labor demand by about 0.48% annually while reinstatement increased it by 0.47%. The authors interpret the small net task-content change as substantial opposing technological changes, not an absence of automation; composition and substitution effects were small.
qs: The top panel in Figure 3 shows that wage bill per capita grew at 2.5% per year during this period.

Between 1947 and 1987, the displacement effect reduced labor demand at about 0.48% per year, but simultaneously, there was an equally strong reinstatement effect, equivalent to an increase in labor demand of 0.47% per year.

kp.k: Recent labor-demand growth slowed as task content deteriorated
kp.d: For 1987–2017, wage bill per capita grew 1.33% annually and essentially stagnated after 2000. The productivity effect slowed to 1.54% annually, versus 2.4% in 1947–1987. Estimated adverse task-content change reduced labor demand by 0.35% annually and 10% cumulatively. Annual displacement increased to 0.7%, while reinstatement declined to 0.35%. Manufacturing displacement was especially pronounced: the main text reports about 1.1% annually or about 30% cumulatively, while the appendix reports 33% cumulatively.
qs: Wage bill per capita grew at a modest 1.33% per year during the entire period and essentially stagnated since 2000.
Cumulatively, changes in the task content of production reduced labor demand by 10% during this period.

During the 1987-2017 period, the displacement effect from automation reduced labor demand in the sector at a rate of 1.1% per year (33% cumulatively), making displacement as important as the price effect during this period (accounting for a cumulative decline of 40%).

kp.k: Proxy correlations support the task-content interpretation
kp.d: The authors compare inferred task-content changes with robot penetration, routine employment and manufacturing automation adoption, finding negative relationships. New-task proxies—new job titles, emerging tasks, newly represented occupations and occupational diversity—have positive relationships. Table 1 uses 61 industries, with robot data mapped from 19 industries, and 148 detailed manufacturing industries for automation-adoption evidence. These are supporting correlations rather than direct causal identification of automation and task creation. Offshoring also correlates with task-content change, but controlling for it does not materially alter reported automation relationships.
qs: These negative relationships remain very similar when we add various control variables, including a dummy for the manufacturing sector as well as imports from China

All four of these measures are meant to capture major changes in the types of activities performed in occupations (then mapped to industries) or the introduction of certain new activities into an industry.

kp.k: Identification depends on assumptions and possible market confounders
kp.d: Separating displacement from reinstatement assumes that an industry does not simultaneously automate and introduce new tasks within a five-year window. If both occur, their offsetting effects make the estimates lower bounds. The authors report robustness to alternative elasticities, technological-growth assumptions, decomposition ordering and inclusion of self-employment income. Nevertheless, changing markups, monopsony and bargaining arrangements that move firms away from their labor-demand curves could confound the inferred task-content changes.
qs: To the extent that there are simultaneous introduction of new automation technologies and new tasks in a given industry within a five-year period, our estimates will be lower bounds both for the displacement and reinstatement effects.
A similar confounding would result if there are changing product market markups.

kp.k: Skills and innovation incentives may explain technological imbalance
kp.d: The authors explicitly lack complete explanations for accelerated automation, weaker reinstatement and slow productivity growth. They favor an incentive-based account over exhausted opportunities for new tasks: preferential taxation of equipment, payroll taxes, technology-company strategies, enthusiasm for removing humans and declining government innovation support may favor automation. They also suggest that skill mismatch can reduce gains from automation and inhibit new tasks. These are proposed mechanisms, not findings established by the decomposition.
qs: Though we do not have complete answers to these questions, our conceptual framework points to a number of ideas worth considering.
Finally, Acemoglu and Restrepo (2018d) suggest there may be a mismatch between the available skills of the workforce and the needs for new technologies.

kp.k: Future work depends on technology mix and policy
kp.d: The authors reject both inevitable mass joblessness and guaranteed labor benefits from technological change. Their conditional forecast is that continued reliance on automation for productivity growth will weaken labor’s relative position unless new tasks or other labor-intensive technologies counterbalance displacement. If innovation has become inefficiently biased toward automation, they suggest removing incentives for excessive automation and rebalancing technological change to improve job creation and productivity.
qs: Our evidence and conceptual approach support neither the claims that the end of human work is imminent nor the presumption that technological change will always and everywhere be favorable to labor.
These might include removing incentives for excessive automation (such as the preferential treatment of capital equipment) and policies designed to rebalance the direction of technological change

cl.s: Concrete claim or prediction about how AI changes legal services, the legal profession, or legal markets (or, for a cross-domain source, its own domain)

pts.k: Acemoglu and Restrepo argue that automation, including AI, displaces labor from tasks, while the creation of new labor-intensive tasks can counterbalance displacement. Productivity growth alone does not guarantee increased labor demand.
pts.d: This is a cross-domain economics source, not a study of legal AI. The authors distinguish automation that transfers tasks from labor to capital from technologies that improve productivity within existing task allocations. In their model, automation reduces the industry's labor share, but its net effect on labor demand depends on whether productivity gains outweigh displacement. New tasks in which humans have a comparative advantage increase labor demand through productivity and reinstatement effects. They suggest that some AI applications could be 'so-so technologies': they substitute for workers but deliver insufficient productivity gains to offset displacement. Their historical interpretation is that stronger displacement, weaker reinstatement and slower productivity growth jointly explain the slowdown in US labor-demand growth. Their forward-looking argument rejects both inevitable joblessness and inevitable benefits to labor: continued wage growth alongside productivity requires new tasks or other technologies that sustain labor's role. They also propose, conditionally, that removing incentives for excessive automation and redirecting innovation could improve job creation and productivity.

cl.s: Evidence basis offered for the claim (data, benchmarks, cases, experience, authority, or none)

pts.k: The claims rest on a task-based economic model, historical examples and a model-based decomposition of US industry data, rather than direct measurement of AI's effects on legal work.
pts.d: The authors use BEA, BLS and NIPA data, consolidating the earlier period into 43 private-sector industries and examining 61 industries in the later period. Labor demand is represented by the wage bill, normalized by population, not by a direct count of jobs displaced. For 1947–1987, they report annual wage-bill growth of 2.5%, a productivity contribution of 2.4%, displacement of approximately −0.48% and reinstatement of +0.47%. For 1987–2017, the corresponding figures are 1.33%, 1.54%, −0.7% and +0.35%; the net task-content contribution is approximately −0.35% annually, or −10% cumulatively. Manufacturing displacement is estimated at approximately −1.1% annually. Task-content changes are inferred from labor-share changes after subtracting estimated substitution effects; they are not directly observed automation events. Correlations with robot penetration, routine employment and manufacturing automation adoption support the displacement interpretation, while new job titles, emerging tasks and occupational diversity support reinstatement. These are supporting correlations rather than a separate causal estimate of AI's impact. Historical examples include agricultural mechanization and the emergence of industrial, clerical and computing-related tasks. Proposed explanations involving tax incentives, technology-company strategies, declining government research support and skill mismatch are presented as possibilities rather than established findings.

cl.s: Stated or implied timeframe, conditions or qualifications under which the claim holds

pts.k: The empirical comparison covers 1947–1987 and 1987–2017; the future-of-work claims are conditional and carry no dated forecast.
pts.d: Writing in 2019, the authors emphasize wage-bill stagnation since 2000. Their predictions depend on the future balance between automation and the creation of labor-intensive tasks. Their basic model assumes that firms find it cost-minimizing to use capital in automated tasks and immediately adopt new tasks. 'New tasks' specifically means tasks in which labor has a comparative advantage, not every new activity introduced by technology. Automation's productivity benefit depends on cost savings: high wages and scarce labor tend to strengthen the positive productivity effect, while low wages and abundant labor can make displacement dominate. Sectoral reallocation can additionally raise or lower aggregate labor demand depending on the labor intensity of expanding sectors. The empirical baseline uses an elasticity of substitution of 0.8 and assumptions about relative factor-augmenting technological growth. Separating displacement from reinstatement assumes that industries do not undertake both within the same five-year window; simultaneous activity makes the estimates lower bounds. Changing product-market markups or labor-market imperfections that move firms off their labor-demand curves could confound the estimates. The paper does not model how wage-bill changes divide between wages and employment.

cl.s: Who is affected and how (market segment, role, firm type, clients, or the public)

pts.k: The affected groups are workers across the economy, especially manufacturing workers and workers performing automatable white-collar tasks; new tasks create different employment opportunities.
pts.d: Acemoglu and Restrepo identify production workers exposed to robotics and automated machinery, alongside white-collar workers in accounting, sales, logistics, trading and some managerial occupations whose tasks are being replaced by software and AI. They identify programming, software and app development, database work, computer security and specialized functions within existing occupations as examples of new tasks. Manufacturing shows especially strong estimated displacement in 1987–2017. Their appendix interprets the association between task-content changes and greater college-educated employment shares as suggesting that automation has mostly substituted for lower-skill workers while new tasks have mostly benefited higher-skill workers. This is an interpretation of industry-level patterns, not an individual-level or AI-specific causal estimate. Workers may experience changes in wages, employment or both; employers gain the ability to substitute cheaper capital for labor. Governments and innovators influence the balance through taxes, research support and technology choices. Although legal services appears as an industry label in an appendix plot, the source does not make a distinct prediction about lawyers, legal clients or legal-service business models.
